blocks.text: You just spent the last lesson learning how to get data into pandas from CSV, Excel, JSON, and SQL. Writing data back out is the mirror image of that, and it comes up just as often. Maybe you cleaned a messy dataset and need to hand it to a teammate. Maybe a script needs to save its output for a web API to serve later. Maybe you are pushing results into a shared database table. Pandas gives you a matching writer for every reader you already know, and just like the readers, the writers have a few parameters and gotchas that genuinely matter.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame flowing through to_csv into a CSV file
blocks.caption: The mirror image of read_csv: a DataFrame becomes a file in one line.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

This lesson covers the four writer functions that mirror the four readers from the last lesson: to_csv, to_excel, to_json, and to_sql. Each one has its own quirks, and a couple of them have genuinely common mistakes that trip up beginners and experienced developers alike. By the end you will know how to write clean, correct output for whoever or whatever consumes it next.
2. Writing CSV Files
df.to_csv() is the one you will reach for the most. Point it at a filename and pandas writes your DataFrame out as comma separated text.
2.1 The index=False Mistake

Here is the single most common mistake beginners make with to_csv. By default, pandas writes your DataFrame's row index as an extra column in the output file, usually labeled Unnamed: 0 when you read it back. Nobody wants that column. It was never data, it was just pandas' internal row labeling, and now it is permanently baked into your CSV.

blocks.alt: The default to_csv call adding an unwanted index column to the output
blocks.caption: Nobody asked for this column. It is the row index, written out by accident.

code.content:
df.to_csv("sales.csv")
# reading it back later gives you an extra "Unnamed: 0" column

blocks.text: The fix is one keyword argument, and you should treat it as the default you always reach for unless you have a specific reason to keep the index.

blocks.alt: to_csv with index=False producing a clean output with no extra column
blocks.caption: This is what you actually want almost every time.

blocks.title: Make index=False a habit
blocks.content: Ask yourself before every to_csv call: does the row index actually mean something I need to keep, like a date or an ID? If not, always pass index=False. It will save you a cleanup step every single time you read the file back.

blocks.text: 2.2 Encoding for Non ASCII Text

If your DataFrame has text with accented characters, non Latin scripts, or currency symbols, you may need to set the encoding explicitly to avoid garbled output or a UnicodeEncodeError on some systems.
utf-8 covers the overwhelming majority of real world text and is a safe default to set explicitly rather than relying on your operating system's default, which is not always utf-8.
3. Writing Excel Files
df.to_excel() writes a DataFrame out as an Excel workbook. It requires the openpyxl package installed alongside pandas, since pandas itself does not know how to speak the xlsx format.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame writing out to a single Excel sheet
blocks.caption: One DataFrame, one sheet, one call.

blocks.text: 3.1 Writing Multiple Sheets Correctly
Say you have two DataFrames, one for sales and one for costs, and you want both in the same workbook on separate sheets. Calling to_excel twice on the same filename does NOT do what you might expect.

blocks.alt: Two separate to_excel calls to the same file overwriting each other instead of adding sheets
blocks.caption: The second call replaces the whole file. The first sheet is gone.

code.content:
df_sales.to_excel("report.xlsx", sheet_name="Sales")
df_costs.to_excel("report.xlsx", sheet_name="Costs")
# report.xlsx now only has the Costs sheet. Sales is gone.

blocks.title: Repeated to_excel calls overwrite the file
blocks.content: Each call to to_excel opens a brand new file on that path by default. It does not know a previous call already put a sheet there. The second call replaces the entire file.

blocks.text: The correct way to write multiple sheets to one file is a pd.ExcelWriter context manager, which keeps the file open across multiple writes.

code.content:
with pd.ExcelWriter("report.xlsx") as writer:
    df_sales.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Sales", index=False)
    df_costs.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Costs", index=False)

blocks.alt: An ExcelWriter context manager correctly writing two DataFrames to two sheets in one file
blocks.caption: Both sheets survive because the writer stays open across both calls.

blocks.text: 4. Writing JSON Files
df.to_json() converts a DataFrame into JSON, which matters constantly when your output needs to be consumed by a web API, a JavaScript frontend, or basically anything outside the Python ecosystem.

The orient parameter controls the shape of the output JSON. There are several options, but records is by far the most common and the most interoperable, since it produces a plain list of objects, one per row, which is exactly what most APIs expect.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame converting to JSON with records orient, producing a list of row objects
blocks.caption: One object per row. This is the shape almost every API expects.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Orient value","Output shape"],"rows":[["records","A list of objects, one per row (most common, most portable)"],["columns","A dict of column name to a dict of index to value"],["index","A dict of index to a dict of column name to value"],["split","A dict with separate columns, index, and data arrays"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Writing to a SQL Database
df.to_sql() writes a DataFrame back into a database table, using the same kind of SQLAlchemy connection or engine object you would use with read_sql.

code.content:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
engine = create_engine("postgresql://user:pass@localhost/mydb")
df.to_sql("orders", engine, if_exists="append", index=False)

blocks.alt: A DataFrame writing into a database table through a SQLAlchemy engine
blocks.caption: The same connection machinery as read_sql, just flowing the other direction.

blocks.text: 5.1 The if_exists Parameter
if_exists tells pandas what to do if the target table already exists, and picking the wrong one can genuinely destroy data.

blocks.content: {"headers":["if_exists value","Behavior"],"rows":[["fail","Raises an error if the table already exists (the safe default)"],["replace","Drops the existing table entirely and recreates it from this DataFrame"],["append","Adds these rows onto the end of the existing table"]]}

blocks.alt: if_exists set to replace silently dropping an existing table's data
blocks.caption: Every row that was already in that table is gone the moment this runs.

blocks.alt: if_exists set to append keeping existing rows and adding new ones
blocks.caption: This is almost always what you actually meant to do.

blocks.title: replace is destructive
blocks.content: if_exists="replace" does not merge or update, it drops the whole table and rebuilds it from scratch using only the rows in your current DataFrame. If that table had other data you were not tracking in this script, it is gone. Default to append or fail unless you are certain replace is what you want.

blocks.text: 6. Choosing the Right Output Format
The right format depends entirely on who or what reads the output next.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Downstream consumer","Best format"],"rows":[["A person opening it manually","Excel (to_excel)"],["Another Python script using pandas","CSV (to_csv) or a binary format like parquet"],["A web API or JavaScript frontend","JSON (to_json, orient records)"],["A shared database other systems query","SQL (to_sql)"]]}

blocks.alt: A decision flow choosing an output format based on who reads it next
blocks.caption: Same DataFrame, different exit depending on the audience.

blocks.text: 7. Worked Example: Writing for Two Different Consumers

Say you just finished cleaning an orders DataFrame. A teammate wants a CSV to poke around in manually, and a separate internal API needs to serve the same data as JSON. You write it out correctly for both in a couple of lines.

code.content:
clean_orders = df[["order_id", "customer", "total", "order_date"]]

clean_orders.to_csv("orders_clean.csv", index=False)

clean_orders.to_json("orders_clean.json", orient="records")

blocks.alt: One cleaned DataFrame written out as both a CSV file and a JSON file
blocks.caption: Same data, two correct outputs for two different audiences.

blocks.text: Notice index=False on the CSV write, keeping the output free of an unwanted extra column, and orient="records" on the JSON write, producing a plain list of row objects that any API consumer can parse without special handling.
8. Recap

items: to_csv writes comma separated text. Always pass index=False unless the index genuinely means something.
to_excel needs openpyxl. Use a pd.ExcelWriter context manager to write multiple sheets to one file, never repeated to_excel calls.
to_json with orient=records produces the most portable, API friendly output shape.
to_sql writes into a database table through a SQLAlchemy connection. Choose if_exists carefully, since replace deletes existing data.
Pick the output format based on who reads it next, not out of habit.
